sentences.text: Alvarezsaurus was a small, bipedal theropod dinosaur measuring between 1 and 1.4 meters long.
This creature possessed a beak and developed feathers covering its body.
Its foot structure was unique among relatives, featuring metatarsal III as the longest bone followed by an unusually long metatarsal IV.
Its leg structure suggests it was capable of running fast.
The species was named by José Bonaparte in 1991 in honor of the historian Don Gregorio Alvarez.
The type specimen was discovered in March 1989 by Jorge Calvo while prospecting along the south coast of the Río Neuquén.
While bone fragments were common finds, the initial discovery involved a 5 cm long white bone fragment found near a light post.
After uncovering part of the fossil, Jorge Calvo confirmed it was the leg of an animal with hollow bones.
In 1991, José Bonaparte published the description of Alvarezsaurus in the Revista del Museo de Ciencias Naturales de Buenos Aires, dedicating the species A. calvoi to Jorge Calvo.
Researchers suggest that Alvarezsaurus may have been insectivorous.
The beak contained sharp teeth, indicating it was a carnivore that likely fed on lizards, insects, and small mammals.
Alvarezsaurus is considered a basal member of the Alvarezsauridae family, preceding better-known relatives like Mononykus and Shuvuuia.
The animal has been classified as either a non-avian theropod or a primitive bird, but the theory linking Alvarezsauridae closely to modern birds remains controversial.
It was once believed that Patagonian Alvarezsaurus taxa were the most basal in their family, but this was refuted by the discovery of the more basal genus Haplocheirus in China.
Alvarezsaurus lived in Argentina approximately 86 to 83 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous.
